questions: Have you been experiencing involuntary shaking or tremor in your hands?
Did the shaking begin suddenly?
Does the shaking affect both hands?
Is the shaking present when your hands are completely at rest?
Does it become worse when you hold your hands out or use them?
Does the shaking stop or lessen when you concentrate on another task?
Does the shaking change markedly in speed or severity during an episode?
Can you voluntarily stop the shaking, even briefly?
Do you have numbness or tingling in either hand?
Have you noticed weakness or loss of dexterity in either arm or hand?
Have you had shaking or abnormal movements elsewhere in your body?
Have you had problems with balance or walking?
Have you had changes in speech, swallowing, vision, or facial movement?
Have you experienced episodes of loss of awareness or blacking out?
Have you had neck pain or pain radiating into either arm?
Did the symptoms begin after an injury, illness, or major emotional stress?
Do you use caffeine, alcohol, recreational drugs, or medicines that make the shaking worse?
Has anyone in your family had a similar tremor or a diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease?
Have you previously been diagnosed with anxiety, depression, or another neurological condition?
Are the symptoms interfering with your daily activities?

results: 1. Comprehensive neurological examination, including cranial nerves, tone, power, reflexes, coordination, gait, and assessment of tremor during distraction and contralateral rhythmic tapping
cranial nerve examination: normal
muscle tone examination: right-sided rigidity with dystonic posturing of the right fingers
limb strength (MRC) examination: normal
deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses: brisk right-sided reflexes with pectoral jerk and positive Hoffman sign
coordination examination (limb and truncal): right-sided limb apraxia with myoclonic jerks
gait observation including turning and doorways: not recorded
tremor characterisation (rest, postural, action): no tremor
2. MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium contrast
MRI brain with gadolinium: markedly asymmetric left-greater-than-right superior parietal and posterior frontal atrophy without abnormal enhancement
3. MRI of the cervical spinal cord with and without gadolinium contrast
MRI cervical and thoracic spine: normal
4. Complete blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, serum glucose, calcium, magnesium, and thyroid-stimulating hormone
serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine: normal
liver function tests: normal
serum calcium, magnesium and phosphate: normal
blood glucose and HbA1c: normal
full blood count, renal and liver profile: normal
TSH / free T4: normal
5. Serum vitamin B12, folate, copper, and ceruloplasmin levels
vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid: normal
serum folate: normal
serum copper and caeruloplasmin: normal
serum ceruloplasmin: normal
6. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography of the affected upper limb
nerve conduction studies: normal
needle electromyography: normal
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Corticobasal degeneration (4-repeat tauopathy) causing corticobasal syndrome with asymmetric cortical myoclonus, dystonia, rigidity, and limb apraxia

ALTERNATIVE 1: Corticobasal syndrome due to Alzheimer disease pathology

ALTERNATIVE 2: Corticobasal syndrome due to frontotemporal lobar degeneration

ALTERNATIVE 3: Focal-onset cortical epilepsy causing epilepsia partialis continua
